title: Buddhism: the first truth
hookLine: life is marked by unsatisfactoriness, and there is a way through (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)

cards: You finally get the thing. The phone, the job, the apartment, the relationship status. For about a week it's wonderful.
Then something is slightly off. The phone is already old. The job has a boss.
The apartment has a neighbor with a drum kit. It isn't a tragedy. Just a faint sense that things never quite land.
After the Buddha woke up, he walked to a deer park and gave his first teaching, and the first of the truths he named there was that feeling. Its name is dukkha.

teach.h: THE DEER PARK, THE FIRST TEACHING.
teach.b: That first teaching was at the Deer Park near Varanasi, to the five companions who had once fasted with him.
Buddhists call it the setting in motion of the wheel of the teaching, and it's recorded in the Samyutta Nikaya, a collection in the Pali Canon.
In it he lays out four noble truths, which later teachers compare to a doctor's diagnosis. First, the illness: dukkha. Second, its cause: craving, a thirst that keeps grasping.
Third, the good news: it can end.

Fourth, the cure: a path, the noble eightfold path. Dukkha is often translated suffering, and that's part of it: birth, aging, sickness and death, being stuck with what you don't want, being parted from what you love.
But the word is wider than pain. It's also stress, friction, unsatisfactoriness: the sense that even pleasant things can't fully satisfy, because they change and pass.
Some teachers explain dukkha with a wheel on a badly fitted axle, so every ride is a little bumpy; scholars doubt that's where the word comes from, but the picture fits.
So the first truth isn't the Buddha saying life is miserable, full stop. It's the first of four. A doctor who names your illness isn't being gloomy; he's starting treatment.
The third truth says it plainly: craving can fade and cease.
The whole point of naming dukkha is the fourth truth: there's a way through.

how: Buddhists study the four noble truths as a foundation of the teaching, and Theravada communities chant the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, on festival days.

o: life's unsatisfactoriness: stress, friction, things that pass
a punishment that comes from bad deeds in a past life
the belief that life is only misery and nothing else

games.q: the four truths — tap the pairs.

s: the first truth says life is only misery
it's a diagnosis, the first of four; the point is the way through.
stress, friction, unsatisfactoriness: even pleasant things change and pass.
the first teaching was given to five former companions
at the Deer Park near Varanasi, to the five who had fasted with him.

games.q: a doctor tells you exactly what's wrong with you. how do you take it?
o: as bad news, and give up.
as the first step: now treatment can start.
games.why: the four noble truths are shaped like a diagnosis: illness, cause, cure, path. naming dukkha is the start of healing, not the end.

practice: Let something that's bothering you come up, small or not, and feel it without the story: not who did what, or why it's unfair. Where is it in your body: tight, heavy, restless?
Name it plainly, this is dukkha, and keep breathing beside it.

wordCard.voice: Dukkha. Pali for suffering, stress, unsatisfactoriness: the first of the Buddha's four noble truths, named so it can be healed. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: suffering, stress, unsatisfactoriness. Sanskrit duḥkha.

carryVoice: Your line: there's a way through. The first truth isn't the last. See you tomorrow.
